items.title: Universal Model for Atoms (UMA) in Computational Asymmetric Catalysis: Comparing Enantioselectivity Predictions
items.abstract_or_text: Universal model for atoms (UMA) was evaluated for predicting enantioselectivity through direct modeling of diastereomeric transition states via conformational ensemble averaging. Across two organocatalytic and two metal-catalyzed transformations, UMA produced experimental selectivity trend with accuracy within 1-2 kcal/mol identifying key structural features governing stereoinduction. Findings discussed here highlight the promise of UMA foundation models as efficient alternatives for expensive quantum chemical methods in mechanistic modeling while also revealing current scope and limitations.

items.title: The Chemistry of the Golgi-Cox Stain
items.abstract_or_text: Our review provides both a theoretical discussion and experimental investigation of the Golgi–Cox stain. While this procedure has been a mainstay in the histologist’s toolkit for centuries and is implemented quite straightforwardly, there is still significant uncertainty around the chemistry. As such, it remains unclear how the stain works and, therefore, how it can be improved to be safer, faster, more reliable and work for larger specimens. Here, we provide technical and chemical considerations supplemented with original experimental observation on tissue clearing methods. Our findings suggest that Golgi–Cox staining cannot be understood as a simple process of stain diffusion, but rather as the outcome of interactions between tissue structure, fixation, chromate-mediated redox chemistry, mercury binding, pH, and cellular composition. Membrane and lipid integrity influence impregnation, while chromate-dependent changes in pH and redox state create the chemical conditions necessary for subsequent mercury reactions whereby only a few neurons fit within this goldilocks zone and are thus successfully stained. Based on our review and our experimental investigations, we propose the first comprehensive mechanism of the Golgi–Cox stain. Our literature survey and experimental data have been synthesised into a resource for both new and experienced practitioners of histology.

items.title: CRISPR-Enabled Transition to Adsorption-Coupled Redox Transport: Toward the Use of Conventional Voltammetry in Electrochemical Biosensors
items.abstract_or_text: Electrochemical aptamer-based (E-AB) biosensors and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) systems have independently advanced molecular diagnostics; however, their integration is less explored. Here, we present a CRISPR-enabled electrochemical sensing platform that directly links CRISPR Cas12a-mediated cleavage of non-specific aptamers to a change of charge transfer at the electrode interface. Methylene blue (MB)-labeled aptamers are immobilized on a gold electrode, forming an electrochemically surface-confined system. Upon target-activated CRISPR cleavage, MB-labeled aptamers are released into the medium, transforming the system into a diffusion-controlled regime. This transition is directly captured through real-time electrochemical monitoring, where alternating current voltammetry reveals a progressive decrease in surface-bound redox reporters, while cyclic voltammetry simultaneously shows an increase in faradaic current due to the accumulation of freely diffusing MB species. Scan rate-dependent analysis confirms a shift from non-ideal surface-limited behavior to diffusion-controlled kinetics, consistent with the Randles–Ševčík relationship. We propose an adsorption-coupled transport model, which supports this interpretation by showing that the plausible post-cleavage voltammetric response is best described by near-surface confinement of released MB-tagged fragments rather than by pure bulk diffusion alone. Dose-response analysis shows that cyclic voltammetry achieves a improved limit of detection (LOD) of approximately , outperforming square wave voltammetry ( across a broader – range), underscoring CV as the more sensitive readout for quantitative biosensing with this platform. By leveraging the exceptional molecular specificity of CRISPR alongside the high sensitivity of E-AB sensors, this work establishes a new sensing paradigm in which conventional steady-state voltammetry can be used for analytical detection.

items.title: Beyond the Kd Gate: Establishing Signal Causality in Electrochemical Aptasensors
items.abstract_or_text: Electrochemical aptasensors combine aptamer-based molecular recognition with electrochemical transduction, but a signal correlated with nominal target concentration alone does not establish aptamer–target binding. Target addition or matrix exposure may alter solution composition, reporter or mediator chemistry, nucleic acid behavior, surface organization, electron-transfer kinetics, interfacial integrity, or surface fouling without aptamer–target complex formation. The Kd gate addresses this upstream problem by requiring auditable, construct-matched verification of aptamertarget binding in homogeneous, non-denaturing solution under sensing-relevant conditions. Passing the gate, however, does not show that an immobilized construct retains recognition or that recognition causes the electrochemical response. We propose a sequential framework in which the Kd gate qualifies the recognition reagent, controlled surface measurements establish retained recognition, transduction measurements determine whether retained recognition generates a measurable response, and signalcausality controls establish whether that response depends on recognition. It distinguishes solutionphase Kd,sol, surface-associated apparent Kd,app, and device-response midpoint C50. It links controls to alternative response pathways and separates claim classes: target-correlated, recognition-linked, mechanistic or thermodynamic, and intended-use. Aminoglycoside and doxorubicin lineages illustrate why sequence conversion, truncation, reporter conjugation, and immobilization require reassessment of recognition and signal attribution. The framework should guide electrochemical aptasensor development with independently supported recognition and intended-use performance claims.

items.title: Judgment by agents, numbers by code: auditable automated speciation analysis towards a chemistry world model
items.abstract_or_text: Chemical speciation governs the reactivity, solubility, and toxicity of a solution, yet assembling speciation calculations from evaluated thermodynamic data remains a manual expert task whose reasoning is discarded once the figure is drawn. To mirror real-world research, automation belongs within a chemistry world model (CWM) where language agents curate and analyze data. As a first module, our agentic framework converts plain-language questions into deterministic equilibrium calculations grounded in NIST Standard Reference Database 46 (SRD-46). Agents resolve intent, curate records, adjudicate duplicates, design calculations, and estimate values beyond database coverage through induction-deduction-validation loops, while deterministic code validates every agentic commitment before it reaches the solver and compacts diagram topology into text readable without a vision stage. Across four case studies of escalating difficulty, quoted constants, patched records, and boundary coordinates reproduced their sources essentially exactly, whereas the same model without the framework missed phases or failed to build a solver. Residual errors surfaced only as auditable narration flaws, from misread topology to a sign-flipped hydrogen-evolution argument. The framework serves as a human-in-the-loop instrument delivering consensus-grade starting points, turning evaluated databases into active discovery instruments, mapping where language-model chemical reasoning still fails, and providing a general agentic template for finetuning.

items.title: Oxidative ArylSF4-tetrafluoroethylation to N-hydroxydicarboximides via in situ generated Silver intermediate from silver(I) fluoride.
items.abstract_or_text: An efficient and streamlined protocol for the ArylSF4-tetrafluoroethylation of N-hydroxyimides has been developed utilizing an in situ generated silver- (1,2,2,2-tetrafluoro-1-(SF4Aryl)ethyl reagent. While traditional methods rely heavily on common fluoroalkylating agents, Aryl-SF4 containing polyfluoroalkylating reagents remain very rare. Herein, we generating a highly reactive silver-tetrafluoroethyl(SF4Aryl) species in situ, followed by its immediate oxidative radical reaction with a diverse range of N-hydroxyimides. Under optimized reaction conditions, using N-Bromosuccinimide as the terminal oxidant, the corresponding Aryl-SF4 containing tetrafluoroethylated products were obtained in moderate to good yields (up to 69 %). This transition-metal-promoted tandem process exhibits broad substrate scope, high functional group tolerance, and eliminates the need for the isolation of unstable organometallic intermediates. Given the high demand for fluorinated motifs in medicinal chemistry and materials science, this operational simplicity offers a powerful, robust strategy for late-stage SF4 containing polyfluoroalkylation.

items.title: Molecular Design and Interface Engineering of Self-Assembled Monolayers for Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells: A Data-Driven Review of Efficiency, Stability and Scalability
items.abstract_or_text: Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) have become indispensable hole-transport layers in inverted perovskite solar cells which enables power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) above 27% in single-junction devices and above 32% in tandems where the tandem devices benefit disproportionately from SAM engineering with certified efficiencies exceeding 31%. In the review eight hypotheses have been proposed including the prediction that bisphosphonic acid SAMs will outperform monophosphonic acid SAMs in thermal stability, glycol ether side chains will improve both PCE and stability and machine learning can identify new SAMs with >27% PCE and >90% retention at 1000 h , the studied researches shows that carbazole-based SAMs with phosphonic acid anchoring groups dominate the field with Me-4PACz and MeO-2PACz . Co-SAM strategies that have hydrogen-bonding additives consistently improve PCE by (1–3)% absolute over single-component SAMs and that bisphosphonic acid anchoring groups are emerging as a way to improve thermal and damp heat stability. Operational stability under maximum power point tracking now exceeds 1000 h for optimized SAM systems though ISOS protocol adoption remains inconsistent.

items.title: Battery models as controlled laboratory methods: simulated results across the operating envelope, code verification and a physics-informed surrogate
items.abstract_or_text: Laboratories increasingly base formulation, protocol and safety decisions on battery models, yet models rarely receive the controls that laboratory methods do: versions, validation on unseen data, reproducible records and verification of the numerical solution. We report a suite of 9 registered models that run inside a laboratory platform (a cell simulator with equivalent-circuit, single-particle, electrolyte-corrected and transient-electrolyte rungs, electrode balancing, pulse and impedance predictors, a plating-limited charging optimiser, a receding-horizon charge controller, an unscented Kalman filter with a stability review, and a mechanistic ageing model), together with the results they produce for a published cell parameterisation and the evidence for trusting those results. Half-way through a 1C discharge, solid diffusion, electrolyte transport and contact resistance cost 85, 49 and 50 mV; the electrolyte-corrected and transient-electrolyte rungs agree within 25 mV at 1C but diverge by 1,051 mV at 3C, where the latter depletes its electrolyte. A plating-limited current staircase reaches 80% state of charge in 22.9 min at 25 ◦C and 83 min at 0 ◦C, and the closed-loop controller needs 21.5 min without a constraint violation, against 28.0 min for the fastest constant current that respects the constraints. Verification against analytic solutions finds the particle solver second-order accurate in its concentration profile but first-order in the surface value that sets the voltage, a reported state of charge that exceeds the charge balance by up to 19.8 points because shells are averaged without volume weights, and a reversed sign in a kinetic term that is numerically negligible. Varying 9 shipped parameters together by a factor of 1.5 gives a 90% voltage band of ±50 mV at 1C, dominated by the positive particle radius and larger than both the discretisation error and the difference between the two electrolyte rungs; at 3C the choice of electrolyte closure outweighs every other source. That budget assumes its parameters reach the decisions a laboratory makes, and they do not: moving the solid diffusivity over two decades changes the delivered capacity at 3C by 34.8 points while leaving the plating limit, the staircase time, the controlled charge time and the least anode potential unchanged in every digit reported, because the charging model reads 2 cell parameters and the controller 2. Where the discharge rung does respond its capacity collapses onto the diffusion time R2/D to within 0.7 points, and because the particle equation is stepped explicitly, the regime of small particles and fast solid diffusion is the most expensive one to simulate. A grid convergence index shows the simulated voltage converging at first order, leaving the default particle grid 30.7 mV from the extrapolated voltage at 3C; polynomial chaos confirms the linear apportioning of variance, and Gaussian-process emulators predict the voltage to 0.8 mV from 100 runs, with no gain from choosing runs by predictive spread. Drawing the same design from a Sobol sequence rather than a Latin hypercube cuts the largest index error at 256 runs from 0.082 to 0.00022, and a reduced two-parameter problem mapped in full on 625 runs puts the sampled estimator within 0.004 of indices computed exactly. Gaussian splatting of simulated fields, implemented for this study, did not compress regular two-dimensional grids better than proper orthogonal decomposition but fitted scattered samples with an error of 9.97 mV against 14.55 mV for triangulation; in three dimensions, across rate and temperature, it beat both decomposition and interpolation. An adaptation of a recent densification strategy from rendering failed at the largest budget; splitting along the axis of largest field change and band-limiting the primitives to the sample spacing made it stable, with a median held-out error over 10 fits of 13.2 mV against 14.4 mV for residual-driven control. Extended to the vehicle, battery power determines only 5 of 6 longitudinal parameters: a physics-informed network fitted it from 8 starting points with the identifiable combinations within 1.9% of the truth, while the masses it returned ranged from 0.79 to 0.98 times the true value. Re-executing the 10 recorded runs from their stored inputs reproduced 9 bit for bit; the exception showed that a run’s code reference names a month, not a version. A physics-informed extreme learning machine, fitted for this study, solves the particle-diffusion problem to a surface-stoichiometry error of 1.2× 10−4 and passes an admission tolerance that the platform’s 14-shell solver fails; a gradient-trained network of the same form improves 21-fold on least squares with the same few fixed features but still fails that tolerance. Toward a digital twin, the suite’s estimator tolerates the drift of an ageing cell, but calibrating the particle diffusivity through the default grid misses it by −17.4%, against −0.5% through the verified surrogate. Governance made each finding checkable; verification made them visible.

items.title: Operational insights from the front lines of OpenADMET: lessons from our blind challenges
items.abstract_or_text: The gap between reported machine learning (ML) model performance in drug discovery and the experience of using these models in live discovery projects remains a major hurdle for the field, because the retrospective nature of most benchmarks makes it difficult to objectively assess progress. To address this gap, OpenADMET has hosted a series of blind challenges to benchmark and advance predictive modeling in absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET). In this Perspective, we distill the operational, strategic, and community-level lessons from our first four blind challenges, providing a practical blueprint for designing and running collaborative machine learning competitions in the life sciences. In addition, we open-source our blind challenge infrastructure and data-validation tools to lower the barrier to entry for hosting rigorous, community-driven competitions and to foster a sustainable framework for collective learning in computer-aided drug discovery.

items.title: Bridging the Training–Application Gap in Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian Learning through Dual-Space Supervision
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting the Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian in density functional theory (DFT) via machine learning offers a promising pathway toward efficient electronic structure modeling. Existing models are typically trained by directly minimizing element-wise Hamiltonian matrix errors, yet a significant trainingapplication gap has been observed between Hamiltonian-space loss and errors in derived electronic properties, limiting their utility in practical applications. Noting that these properties are functions on the state space obtained by solving the Hamiltonian eigenvalue problem, this gap can be traced to a misalignment of the error metrics on the Hamiltonian space and its induced state space. The operator-tostate mapping is highly anisotropic, such that Hamiltonian errors of comparable numerical magnitude can induce markedly different downstream property errors. Motivated by the Hamiltonian–state variational duality rooted in Lieb’s convex formulation of DFT, we introduce Dual-Space Loss (DSLoss) to bridge this training–application gap. By leveraging error metrics in both spaces, DSLoss allows Hamiltonian optimization to account for errors in both the predicted operator and its induced state. Across molecular benchmarks, DSLoss consistently improves a broad range of derived properties over conventional element-wise supervision. On the challenging ∇2DFT benchmark, electron density and total energy errors are reduced by factors of 40 and 500, respectively, relative to the strongest competing method. The resulting model also extrapolates robustly to molecules containing up to twice as many heavy atoms as those encountered during training, achieving more than an order-of-magnitude lower errors for multiple properties and substantially outperforming direct density prediction models and endto-end property predictors. Moreover, the model enables stable molecular dynamics simulations with accurate energetics, forces, and vibrational dynamics. These results show that DSLoss addresses an unrecognized bottleneck limiting operator-prediction models across diverse downstream tasks, thereby advancing scalable and reliable electronic structure modeling.

items.title: From sequences and structures to fitness, folding and function: challenges in the age of AI
items.abstract_or_text: Deep-learning models have transformed our ability to predict the phenotypic effects of sequence perturbations. Protein language models (pLMs) score the evolutionary propensity of any amino-acid substitution, emerging as fast and accurate predictors of fitness changes. Inverse-folding (IF) models add structural information and are powerful alternatives for estimating folding-stability changes. But these likelihoods are imperfect and sometimes biased predictors of the biological quantities they are used to measure. Scaling pLMs has shown that bigger models do not always outperform smaller ones. IF models sometimes read sequence conservation as a stability constraint, which leads to biases when this signal is used to isolate functional contributions beyond folding. We review here the strategies emerging to mitigate, and where possible overcome, these limitations. Highlights:- Scaling protein language models does not close the likelihood–fitness gap - Inverse-folding models can read functional conservation as lost stability - Disentangling function from stability inherits both biases - Emerging strategies are attempting to address these issues

items.title: Phase-field modeling of porosity formation and evolution during hydrogen-based iron oxide reduction
items.abstract_or_text: Hydrogen-based direct reduction of iron oxides (HyDRI) offers a low-emission route to solid-state ironmaking by replacing carbon-based reductants with hydrogen. The mass loss associated with oxygen removal generates porosity. The evolving pore network influences reduction kinetics through changes in transport pathways and internal reaction surfaces. Here, we develop a phase-field framework that couples solid-state oxygen transport, the wüstite–ferrite transformation, and pore evolution during the rate-controlling step of HyDRI. Pore generation follows the local transformation rate at the advancing reaction front, whereas surface diffusion redistributes existing porosity. The newly formed solid–pore interfaces provide additional oxygen-removal sites, coupling pore evolution back to front propagation. The simulations show that increasing reduction-generated porosity drives a transition from isolated pores to connected channels, raising the fraction of pore space connected to the external surface from approximately 7% to 97%. Additional internal reaction surfaces shorten the time to 90% reduction by approximately 15%, demonstrating how pore formation accelerates further reduction. Faster front propagation preserves fine, tortuous pores, whereas faster surface diffusion promotes smoothing and coarsening. The resulting structures differ by more than a factor of two in the solid–pore interfacial length available for oxygen removal, even at the same reduction-generated porosity. Pore connectivity and the internal surface available for reaction therefore depend on reduction history and cannot be inferred from porosity alone. These findings provide a physical basis for linking local pore evolution to gas access and overall reduction kinetics at larger scales.
